content: Smallpox was officially eradicated by 1980, but concerns about its potential use as a bioweapon have renewed interest in the development and evaluation of protective vaccines. As a result, both stockpiled vaccines derived from calf lymph and newer cell-cultured vaccines have been studied to provide critical information for smallpox emergency response plans. Additionally, newer vaccines that are non-replication competent are under development. The primary objective of this research was to evaluate the effectiveness of smallpox vaccines in preventing the disease, their ability to induce immunity, and the associated adverse events. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted in December 2006 across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Infectious Diseases Group Specialized Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, LILACS, and Current Controlled Trials. Index Medicus was also hand-searched. Furthermore, in December 2005, three vaccine safety databases were reviewed. The study included randomized controlled trials comparing smallpox vaccines to placebo, other smallpox or non-smallpox vaccines, no intervention, or different doses of the same vaccine. Participants of all ages who received smallpox vaccination were included. The quality of the trials was independently assessed by two authors, and data were extracted and analyzed. Dichotomous data were combined using a risk ratio with a random-effects model. A total of ten trials involving 2,412 participants were included in the analysis. The vaccines studied included first-generation vaccines derived from calf lymph (such as Dryvax, APVS, Lancy-vaxina, and Lister) and second-generation cell-cultured vaccines (such as ACAM and CCSV). These vaccines were tested at various dilutions. All undiluted vaccines produced a reaction in 95% of vaccinated individuals, as evidenced by the development of pustules and immunogenicity. Vaccines diluted to a 1:10 ratio were also fully effective, provided the initial concentration was appropriately defined. Serious adverse events were reported in 1% to 2% of participants. Fever occurred in 11% to 22% of individuals, while headaches were reported by approximately half of the participants. Fever was less common with the administration of newer vaccines, but the frequency of headaches was similar between older and newer vaccines. The findings indicate that stockpiled vaccines have retained their immunogenicity over time, and newer cell-cultured vaccines demonstrate comparable success rates and immunogenicity. Both firstand second-generation vaccines, when diluted to at least a 1:10 ratio, were as effective as undiluted vaccines in terms of clinical success and immunogenicity. Dilution did not reduce the frequency of adverse events. The success rate and immunogenicity were similar in individuals who were naive to vaccination and those who had been previously vaccinated. However, previously vaccinated individuals experienced fewer adverse events. The rate of adverse events observed in this review highlights the need for further development and refinement of smallpox vaccines to improve their safety profile.
